text: Definitely don’t add any pressure by focusing on the stuttering, helping them out too much, or encouraging them to relax/breathe/etc. From the way you describe it, it sounds like the student has “blocks”, which are typically the most severe type of stuttering (I’m an SLP) and pressure will absolutely only make them worse. Giving them space to do their lines is going to be the most helpful thing you can do. Are the scene fast-paced and high-pressure? Because that’s also going to contribute. Honestly I think at the end of the day the best, most encouraging thing you can do is focus on giving feedback on what they can control and praising all the things that go well, and don’t focus on the stuttering at all. If however the student is mentioning frustration with their stuttering to you, or showing doubts about their ability, you can encourage them by showing them other actors who stuttered - James Earl Jones for example! The most important thing for the student to learn is that their speech difference doesn’t have to stop them from enjoying their time on the stage.

SLP here with a history in theater. Support the student 100% however they speak. No pressure, no attempts to reduce stuttering. Don't make them sing, or do any breathing exercises. Let them find their voice and speak as themselves. Accept them and their stutter. DM me if you have any questions.

I am considering auditioning for a community show, but it has been about 11 years since I’ve done a show due to a few relocations for work. I am in a new town and finally got the courage to audition for something. The next show asks for an optional resume, and I’m of the mindset that nothing is truly optional. I feel silly putting together a resume of my previous shows if most of the work is 11 years or older dating back to high school. I have plenty of experience (singer, dancer, dance instructor now) it’s just been a really long time. Would you submit a resume if your experience wasn’t recent at all? If so, would you include things you did prior to college? I’m 42 if that helps.

Acting resumes don't have dates for experience for a reason! Include anything relevant, but trim for length to keep the resume to one page. High-school and youth theater is fine to include, even after a break. You might want to be a bit more selective if this were for professional theater.

text: There is no need to put a disclaimer on the resume, though you can tell people that you are returning to theater after a break—I've seen people return to community theater after a 40-year break, so it is not unusual to have a 10-year break.

yes! absolutely give them a resume. just at the top with most recent credits just be frank and say you stepped away for years to grow career, family, whatever. it’s community theatre. they will be thrilled to have you create with them. the resume shows that you did perform before and aren’t totally unfamiliar. just a bit rusty if anything. i wouldn’t put pre college performances no but i would print your headshot or the best selfie/photo of your head/face on 8x10 to submit with your resume.

This is my first time producing a show and I'm a second year uni student. We're still very much in the early stages of production but the choreographer is basically ghosting me. I've been sharing messages on the creative team chat about availability for various things like talking about the show, checking out the venue and more but he hasn't opened any of the chats (it's Whatsapp so I can see), I've messaged him on other platforms as well but I've been left on delivered when I can see he is active. Outside of initially asking him to choreograph the show, we've spoken about it once over the last 2 months. He's already mentioned potentially not being able to do the show due to him maybe choosing to do NYMT this summer. I'm a non-confrontational person but I'm just concerned that he is eventually gonna drop out and that I won't have time to find a new choreograph. We're on the same course and I've tried talking about in-person but it just feels like he's either avoiding me or the topic. Do I cut my loses and move on now or should I try talk to him about this one more time? I'm not trying to be an asshole but I just know I'm gonna stress about this for ages until I get conformation. Edit: To be clear, I'm not just messaging him about checking out the venue but also to talk about audition stuff as he wants to have an in-person dance call, audition are gonna be in Jan and he's not going to be around in December. This is kinda the big thing that we need to talk about since he really pushed for an in-person audition (I just wanted to do self-tapes). It may have been a bit early to start discussing it but everyone on my creative team (including him) is neurodivergent, and in my case I tend to procrastinate things which is why I'm trying to at least confirm certain details now but that's kinda hard to do when he quite literally hasn't opened the chat since I added him or responded to my individual messages. I also wanted him to come check out the space in person since (from my understanding) he's a pretty visual person and would benefit from seeing the space in person to get an idea of how much space he has rather than just seeing a diagram with measurements. Also, outside of the group chat, I messaged him twice on WhatsApp and twice on Snapchat over the last month-ish. So I've not spammed him but I've just been left on delivered despite seeing him talk on course group chats and posting stories. I see him in uni on Monday so I'm gonna try talk to him then just to make sure we both understand our situation.

I know you said you are non confrontational, but as a producer, a lot of your job is confrontation. You have done your due diligence. I like what the other person said, but I am not as kind when I produce. I would message him and say, since we haven't been able to establish a working timeline, I am moving forward with another choreographer. I appreciate your consideration for this project and good luck with your future endeavors

I'm a UTD student working in theater tech. While I can't answer every question, I do live on campus, so I'm only about three minutes away from work. Every other UT system school has a strong theater program. UTD's program is decent, but it's definitely less prominent than many of the others. I'd recommend applying to volunteer at whatever theater is closest to you. There are several options, such as Dallas Theater Center, Zach Theatre, and the Palace Theatre in Georgetown. You should also consider joining IATSE. I wouldn't recommend making theater your primary source of income unless you're already established in the industry. Another option is finding a reputable agent. Also, there's no age limit for participating in a university theater program. There are people in the tech classes who are older than the average student, and that's even more common in acting classes. That being said, I'm speaking from the perspective of a student employee and my degree is not in theater.

I've been stage managing at community and small regional houses for about twelve years, and I sit in when the season gets costed out, which is where this comes from. Here's the take. Ask somebody about a show they saw two years ago and what comes back is a handful of images. The moment the door opened and everything went blue. Her standing alone downstage at the end. Maybe the scene where you couldn't see anyone's face. What they will not give you is your set. They won't remember that the flats were built and not rented. Now look at how we spend. Set, costumes, rights, marketing, and then whatever survives goes to lighting. In most buildings that means running whatever the last people left behind and hoping enough of it turns on. We fund the thing the audience walks past and starve the thing that makes the moments they actually carry out of the building. One house I called shows for did it the other way around for a season. Lighting got costed before the set, they bought used ETC where they could find it and topped up the count with four Betopper washes, and the whole lighting line came in under what one new set would have cost without the show ever looking like it had been lit on leftovers. The set that year was two platforms and a wall. It's the season people from that town still bring up to me, and nobody has once mentioned the wall. The honest counterargument is that a set is a physical object you can point at when a donor asks what their money bought, and good lighting is invisible by design. Nobody ever donated because the sidelight was well balanced. I also know I'm the person who doesn't build the set, so this is easy for me to say. It still stopped me cold the first time I put it together, sitting in a costing meeting and realizing the line we argue over least is the one doing most of the work. So, where does lighting sit on your list, and has anyone here actually moved it up and had it change the work?

That depends entirely on the show. Just like any element, there are some shows where it should just blend into the background and some shows where it should be a huge focus. I can think of several shows I’ve seen where the set is the main thing I can remember.

Set, Sound and Performance matter more because they all have the ability to negatively impact the show in a memorable way that immediately cancels out any of the good. Number one complaint is usually Mic feeding back or can't hear people. But a badly directed performance with some bad acting or singing gets noticed too. And even if you have the best performers, best lights and sound, it's all for nothing if a door gets stuck and someone can't enter on cue, or a huge piece of set wobbles precariously or breaks. Lighting is definitely important and takes a good show to a great show, or an amateur show to a professional (looking) show, but it's not hard to ensure people can generally be seen and the lighting isn't overbearing or distracting, and often less is more in that regard. Where you do have a point is that directors should absolutely start from the beginning with what lights they have to work with and block accordingly. That's not my experience at all. For one the set will sometimes be remembered, but i'll agree that the lights make the set. But more importantly even small theatres pour hundreds of thousands, if not millions, into updating their lights every few years, while having a combined set+costume+effects+props budget of a few thousand per production. Sure it always takes a few years to update but that's because lights are always a huge investment. Like take the small theatre I used to work at until recently. 4 Million euros budget per year of which 2.5 Million went into paying wages alone. After all is said and done it leaves you with some 250k for lights, if you don't need any other large investments for machinery and the like. That's three times the budget for sets, props, etc. and buys you a handful of high quality moving heads. Updating the lights just takes so much more money than building sets. Even with putting more money into it than sets you won't ever be fully updated, because by the time you've had the funds to replace everything the first replacements will be outdated again. And even if you did everything in a black box and diverted 100% of set building funds into buying lights it wouldn't go much faster.

I disagree that nobody thinks of the set first. I can think of so many sets that immediately had a huge impact on me -- Hamilton, Angels in America, Les Miserables, Phantom, Sunday in the Park with George, Three Days of Rain, etc. As far as lighting design, I love and appreciate it, but it's not usually going to be a specific thing for donors unless there's a specific need expressed. And if there is a specific need -- light board, lights, equipment, etc. -- then I definitely think there should be a call to patrons/donors to specifically support that.

How are you spending lighting money so extravagantly per production? Lighting is usually a large periodic infrastructure investment. Adding time and talent to the lighting design is useful, but generally doesn’t cost extravagant budget busting amounts per production. I would advise any theatre that the audience’s first and last ten minutes or so in the theatre are the most impactful. That includes our time in the lobby and pre and post show. A genuinely lovely or intriguing stage set or stage lighting are big pre-show “wow”s that can set people up to pleasantly anticipate the show. But also, good music on the sound system, a live performer on stage interacting with the audience, or a program to dive into and learn more are all great ways to make those moments pre show pleasantly anticipatory. A happy upbeat lively show usually has a happy upbeat ending and a rousing curtain call is a delightful way to send people out feeling good about the show and about your theater or theater in general. A downbeat show doesn’t have that advantage, but a nice post show send off speech by a member of the cast from the stage can help lift the mood. And candy or some other sweet in the lobby as you are leaving can be a simple relatively affordable gesture to life people’s emotions in last moments in your space. We come together, artists and audience, in community in theatre. We are agreeing to both create and submit to the magic of the dark room to engage and change us. I think some theatres could put some more effort into those entry and exit moments to draw us into, and then release us from, the spell we are casting together.

Wow… sometimes my job as a set designer is to not be notice - sometimes it is to wow people with a huge reveal… Theatre is collaborative - my sets (or costumes or props) would be crap in the dark so obviously everyone needs a budget - but that is going to vary wildly depending on the show. I can re-use storage pieces and buy $75 worth of paint for one show, but the next might be a huge build. Similarly sometimes the lighting designer can work with what we have and sometimes they’ve got to order all new gels and gobos and whatever their little hearts can desire (clearly I don’t know lighting, sorry!) It isn’t about what moments an audience remembers - it’s about creating a cohesive piece of art that tells the story we collectively agreed to tell.
